chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the man who touches the deceased, is it befitting for him to perform ghusl because of it? He said: No. Rather, that is for the human being alone.
He said: And I asked him about the man whose garment is touched by the body of the deceased, so he said: He washes what the garment was touched by.
ai.seo_question: Does touching a dead body require ghusl in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the fiqh of minor impurity (najāsah) versus major ritual bath (ghusl), establishing that contact with a corpse does not trigger the obligation of ghusl unless accompanied by seminal emission or other specific conditions. This ruling distinguishes the physical state of the deceased from the spiritual state of the living, emphasizing that only the specific area of the garment or body in contact requires washing rather than a full ablution or bath. This principle is foundational in Shia jurisprudence for determining the level of purification required after handling the dead.
